But here is the thing the aggregate framing hides, and the reason this chapter is built the way it is: the discount is not a weather system that fell evenly on the creative economy. Duration varies by sector — a AAA game is a seven-year claim, a feature three to five, a television commission one to three, a venue a different kind of claim entirely — and moats vary with it. So the repricing has drawn a map. Meanwhile the pull on the far side keeps strengthening: the generative-content market that stood at $14.8 billion in 2024 is projected to quintuple within five years, with forecasters sizing it at $80 billion by 2030 — a gravitational mass every content pound must now be weighed against.326 AI has not made creative investment uniformly scarcer. It has re-sorted it, sector by sector, by duration and by moat, and the four sectors this book lives across — games, film, television, immersive — have received four different verdicts.

And across all four, watch the direction of the money that stays, because it answers the question I am asked most often: if capital is fleeing the work, what is it buying instead? It is buying the layer underneath the work — the tools, the models, the training data, the infrastructure. Long the means of production, short the products.

Music, as ever, got its verdict first: the shortest cycle in the creative economy took the flood first, and Chapter 5 recorded the result — a majority of the upload pipeline now synthetic, a consumption share pinned in the low single digits, and the money pooling in the tools rather than the tracks. The tooling numbers have only steepened since that chapter’s edition went to press: Suno, which raised $250 million at a $2.45 billion valuation in the week Issue 8 shipped, closed $400 million at $5.4 billion by the week of Issue 32 — a valuation that more than doubled in seven months while genuine human listening to fully synthetic music stayed under one per cent of streams — and Apple quietly made an AI audio company, Qai, its reportedly second-largest acquisition ever at $1.6 billion.327 Hold that shape in mind. It is the preview. What follows is the anatomy: what AI has actually done to the investment case in each of the four screen-and-experience sectors, read from the allocation data rather than the press releases — and then, at the end, what to do about it, because the answer this chapter builds to is instruments, not vibes.

Games: the longest bet in the building

Games carry the longest production cycles in the creative economy, so if the duration discount is real, games should show the deepest cut. They do.

Venture investment in games collapsed from a 2021 peak of roughly $12.5 billion to $2.54 billion in 2024 — an eighty per cent drawdown.328 Here are the receipts the opening promised, dates first, before AI takes the blame it has been eagerly assigned: the collapse began in 2022 — before any tool existed that could plausibly threaten a AAA pipeline — and the roughly forty-five thousand jobs lost across the sector between then and mid-2025, the wave peaking in early 2024 and decelerating since, belong mostly to the monetary story.329 AI arrived mid-contraction and became the narrative: the all-purpose justification, as Chapter 14 documented from inside the org charts, for cuts that rates had already ordered. The labour market priced the resulting spread with brutal clarity in the newsletter’s very first week: as the layoff wave rolled through the studios, Netflix was advertising up to $840,000 a year for a director of generative AI for games.330

What AI changed is where the surviving money goes. The 2026 recovery is genuine and genuinely instructive: Drake Star recorded a twelve-month funding high above $2.5 billion in the second quarter — concentrated not in games but in AI tooling, advertising infrastructure and user-generated-content platforms.331 PitchBook’s commentary was unusually blunt for a data house: gaming venture capital now flows to the companies building AI rather than to games, investors treating the sector as a proving ground for generative infrastructure and “funding the tooling layer ahead of individual-game content.”332 Sixty-one per cent of all global venture capital went to AI firms in 2025;333 every pound contemplating a games position is benchmarked against that, and a seven-year content bet is not merely judged risky against it. It is judged slow — an indictment independent of any view about the work. You can watch the re-sorting week by week in the newsletter’s own record, which through the winter and spring read like a tape of the tooling layer capitalising while new-studio content rounds went missing: Fifth Door’s $20 million for AI game creation, Razer’s $600 million pivot to AI gaming, Sett’s $30 million Series B for automated game marketing, Astrocade’s $56 million for interactive AI, Aippy announcing tens of millions at a $250 million valuation, Welevel’s $8.5 million for an AI-built survival game — a round or two most weeks, and barely a conventional content greenlight among them.334

The darkest datum in the sector, though — the one I keep returning to — is an arc the newsletter caught at both ends. In October, Issue 3 flagged a $134 million seed round, unusual size for the category, for General Intuition: a startup training agentic AI on video-game clips, teaching machines spatial reasoning from recordings of people playing. By the time Issue 36 went out in the summer, the same company had raised $320 million at a $2.3 billion valuation, and a smaller specialist, Origin Lab, had taken $8 million to mine training data from games.335 By July the category had a name and a pipeline: Cambridge’s Worldmodeldata raised £7 million to turn video games into AI training data, Meta shipped a consumer app — Pocket — that turns every play session into training data by design, and open libraries of raw gameplay hours began circulating on Hugging Face.336 Sit with what that arc means. The fastest-appreciating asset to come out of the games industry in 2026 is not a game. It is the exhaust — the behavioural data trail of humans at play, harvested to train agents for the physical world. Capital has found a way to be long the games industry that requires no bet on any game shipping at all, and it is paying frontier-lab multiples for the privilege. If you want a single image of the duration discount at work, it is this: seven-year artefacts unfundable, while the by-product of their audiences’ attention commands $2.3 billion.

Then, in the space of ninety days this summer, the sector staged the whole argument as theatre, in two capital events that should be read as a diptych.

The first ships this November: Grand Theft Auto VI — greenlit thirteen years ago, in a world that contained no transformer architecture, no diffusion models and no consumer generative video, and arriving now as what the analysts at Drake Star call likely the largest game launch in history.337 It is the cleanest surviving specimen of the underwriting world this chapter opened by describing: a decade-plus claim, committed blind, about to pay out anyway. And it is paying out not because the world proved predictable — by launch day the world contained a synthetic actress with a talent agency — but because the asset was moated in the one currency the transition cannot inflate: a fandom, a canon, a world people live inside and want more of from these makers. Even the publisher’s own leadership frames the technology as unable to originate the franchise — while, as Issue 24 reported and Chapter 14 dissected, laying off its entire seven-year-old internal AI team in favour of off-the-shelf tooling.338 Read those two facts together and you get the franchise position in miniature: AI as commodity input, the world and its audience as the asset.

But carry with you a correction the next chapter will earn in full, because capital is currently half-right in a way that will hurt the half that’s wrong. The moat that survives the flood is fandom, not formula — and the AAA titles whose value is production polish on the fifth iteration of an open-world template are, precisely because the formula is what the models learn first, the most exposed content in the sector. An allocator who reads “sequels are safe” out of GTA VI is buying the wrong asset with the right instinct.

The second event closed on the fourth of August, ten days before this chapter’s edition date: Electronic Arts left the public markets in a $55 billion transaction — the largest leveraged buyout in history — with Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund taking 93.4 per cent, Silver Lake 5.5, Affinity Partners 1.1, on roughly $36 billion of equity and $20 billion of debt.339 Two features of that deal belong in this chapter’s evidence file. One: the identity of the buyer. When venture capital flees duration, the assets do not evaporate — they migrate to the one class of allocator whose horizon exceeds the uncertainty. A sovereign wealth fund executing a generational diversification strategy is, almost by definition, the natural holder of the Seven-Year Problem: it is the only balance sheet in the market for whom 2033 is the near term. Two: the role of AI in the underwriting. Twenty billion dollars of debt has to be serviced by margins, and the consortium’s own framing leans on heavy investment in AI applications across a live-service portfolio of seven hundred million players — a thesis the banks had already sized, with analysts talking of $22 billion in AI-driven profit headroom across the industry.340 Which is to say: in the largest games transaction ever done, AI appears not as the existential threat to the asset but as the margin story that makes the leverage add up. The bear case and the bull case are the same technology, held by different balance sheets at different durations.

That is the games verdict, stated plainly. Venture money has repriced the sector’s long tail to near-zero and rotated into picks, shovels and exhaust; the long-duration assets that still clear the discount are carried by fandom moats and sovereign patience; and the middle — the new studio, the original IP, the first game — is where the discount lands with full force. Keep hold of that last clause. It recurs.

Film: the machinery seizes

Film’s cycles are shorter than games’ — three to five years from development to release — but film depends more than any other sector on a lattice of intermediated finance: banks, presales, co-productions, completion bonds, slate vehicles. And the most consequential thing AI has done to film investment is not to change anyone’s opinion. It is to seize the machinery.

Start at the dullest, most load-bearing joint. Banks, presale buyers and co-production partners release funds against completion bonds; bonds are underwritten against known production functions — a script, a schedule, a director with a track record, a physical process whose failure modes a century of claims data has catalogued. As of this year, no major bond company has published underwriting criteria for AI-native production, where the “script” may be a prompt architecture and the “schedule” a generative pipeline run — which locks AI-first features out of institutional finance altogether and makes them dependent on exactly the fast, unstructured capital that arrives on a keyword and can leave on one.341 Read the bond gap as epistemology, not paperwork. The institutions whose entire function is converting uncertainty into priced risk are declining to perform the conversion, because they cannot yet build the actuarial table. When insurance cannot form, the financial system is telling you, in its own dialect, that it has met genuine Knightian uncertainty.

The spread that seizure creates was measured, perfectly, by one man in February. Roger Avary — an Oscar-winning screenwriter with three decades of relationships — described how years of failing to finance conventional features through conventional channels ended the moment he founded an AI-branded production company: three films funded almost overnight, on his own account essentially because the word AI was attached.342 One anecdote, but the newsletter’s record shows it was no outlier — it was the visible tip of an asset class forming. Wonder, the British AI film studio, took a £9 million seed in October that Issue 5 logged as a curiosity; by the time Issue 30 shipped in May, Deadline was profiling it as the $50 million studio styling itself the A24 of AI production. Filmology Labs announced itself as a $250 million studio built for AI-era content. Singapore’s Video Rebirth raised $50 million chasing studio-grade AI video. A married couple got $6 million out of Y Combinator on a pitch deck that literally wedded AI and filmmaking.343 Position Two of Chapter 7’s map — the AI-native studio — is now a funded category, capitalised at nine figures, while the conventional independent market has moved, in the trade’s own language, from momentum to scrutiny: harder questions, earlier, about comps, incentives, attachments and proof.344

Underneath the spread sits a cost curve whose steepness deserves plain statement, because it is the saturation mechanism of Chapter 5 arriving in film’s economics. By spring, Seedance 2.0 had pushed generation cost below fourteen cents a second of video.345 A feature-length AI film reportedly made for around two thousand dollars premiered at Tribeca.346 And at Cannes — the datum I found most clarifying all year — the Wall Street Journal profiled a competition film that cost $500,000, of which $400,000 was AI compute: a production budget in which the compute line has swallowed the crew list.347 The mid-market is trying the hybrid version — Killing Satoshi, a $70 million feature with a name cast, is being made with heavy AI use precisely to make its budget close348 — and the tooling vendors are selling the saturation thesis as a promise: Runway’s chief executive pitches a world where Hollywood makes fifty films instead of one $100 million blockbuster.349 Fifty films for the price of one is a marvellous sentence for a tools company and a terrifying one for anybody whose business model depends on the scarcity of the one.

Where the studio money has gone instead is the barbell, and one balance sheet states it more cleanly than any analyst note. The two largest acquisitions in Netflix’s history are now a catalogue of beloved children’s IP — the Roald Dahl Story Company, roughly $700 million in 2021 — and a sixteen-person AI post-production startup, Ben Affleck’s InterPositive, first flagged in Issue 20 at a reported $600 million and confirmed — in the securities filing the newsletter caught in Issue 39 — at $587 million cash.350 Proven story-worlds at one end; the machinery that makes everything else cheap at the other; and a walking-away from most of what lies between. The tooling end is where film’s capital velocity now lives, and no company demonstrates it like Higgsfield, whose arc the newsletter tracked in real time: an $80 million raise at a $1.3 billion valuation in January; $200 million of revenue within nine months of launch by February; half a billion in revenue and talk of a $5 billion round by midsummer.351 No content business on earth compounds at that speed — which is precisely the comparison every limited partner is now making. Runway sits at $5.3 billion with dedicated film funds and a $40 million Japanese expansion; Luma closed $900 million Saudi-led; Kuaishou’s Kling raised a record $2.8 billion in July;352 Adobe and Google stood up film grants; A24’s DeepMind investment demonstrated, via instant fan backlash, that even the arthouse brand premium is now entangled with the provenance politics of Chapter 13.353

There is a shadow over that compounding, though, and an investment chapter would be malpractice not to price it. Every pure-play on the list — Higgsfield, Runway, Luma, Pika and the rest of a leaderboard that reorders itself roughly quarterly — is selling, at bottom, a model. And the two most consequential owners of video models sell no model at all. Google ships Veo through Gemini, YouTube and its cloud, wrapped in the service agreements, enterprise controls and SynthID provenance that procurement departments actually buy, while ByteDance’s Seedance and Kuaishou’s Kling arrive subsidised by short-video empires that need the firehose fed, collapsing the price floor towards pennies a second as they come.354 For the platforms, in other words, the model is not a business; it is a feature of a distribution empire — and features priced as businesses is a category for which venture history knows exactly one ending. Sora is what that ending looks like at frontier scale: the most-hyped video product of its generation, reportedly burning compute at a daily rate its lifetime revenue never approached, folded in March by the one lab with a claim to the best model but no distribution economics to carry it — in the same spring that Higgsfield’s valuation quadrupled.355 A five-billion-dollar round and a shutdown, twelve weeks apart, inside one asset class: that is the duration distribution at the tooling end, stated plainly. Nor is the mortality confined to the frontier: in August, Reforged Labs — an AI ad-creative startup serving the games market — shut down with its chief executive conceding that “the gap we were selling into is closing”: the models were eating his market faster than he could sell into it.356 The model is the shortest-lived asset in the entire creative stack — the thirteen-year game will outlive every model used to build it, several generations over — and the moats that survive at this end are the ones this book keeps finding everywhere else: distribution, workflow relationship, and clean, licensed, provenance-bearing data. (And, in one small August datapoint I cannot resist recording: taste — Design Arena’s founders raised $7.9 million that month to bring exactly that to AI models, the age of the Why arriving as a seed round.357) The barbell’s safe end is a knife-fight priced like a haven.

And notice the strange, telling instrument that has bloomed in the underwriting vacuum: the prize. Dubai launched a $1 million AI short-film award with Google; the XPRIZE Future Vision competition put up $3.5 million; Astana opened a $1 million prize fund; Luma ran a $1 million global brief; Adobe attached $10 million in grants to its film push; Google gave Sundance $2 million for AI literacy; Runway bankrolls films directly through its Hundred Film Fund.358 By August the pattern was compounding: Higgsfield opened a Global Film Festival with a $1 million prize pool and half a million dollars for first place — having open-sourced its own 95-minute AI feature as the calling card359 — and the Raindance festival launched a development fund and hub for indie filmmakers with the AI platform IMGN.360 Festivals and tool vendors, standing in for a financing system. When the modern instruments — bonds, presales, slate finance — cannot form, financing regresses to its pre-modern shapes: patronage, commission, and the prize. It is a rational adaptation and an indicting one. The film verdict, then: plumbing seized, spreads inverted towards the AI-branded, an AI-native studio class capitalised into existence, the cost curve collapsing under the mid-market, studio capital barbelled between catalogue and machinery — and the mid-budget original, the tranche the whole intermediated lattice existed to finance, left holding the discount, or queueing for a prize.

Television: duration arbitrage

Television ought, on the duration logic, to be the least disturbed screen sector: commissions run one to three years, catalogues amortise fast, and the streamers’ pipelines are annual. Instead television is where the repricing is most visible — because television is short-cycle enough for allocation decisions to show up in the data within quarters, and because the sector was already contracting when AI arrived: the streamers’ pivot from growth-at-any-cost to margin discipline had already cut scripted volume from its 2022 high, and by this winter the trade press was describing feature and episodic shoots drying up in Los Angeles as a fact of life rather than a cycle.361

Inside the pipeline, AI’s arrival looks like Chapter 7’s Position One map executed at speed: Amazon’s internal AI Studios unit and the publicly disclosed 350-plus generative VFX shots in House of David; Netflix’s INKubator, an AI-native animation unit reporting into the same commissioning structure as the live-action slates; Disney’s enablement office and advertiser-facing generation tools — and, on the revenue side, AI agents deployed to grow Netflix’s $3 billion advertising business, the margin story running a floor below the commissioning story.362 The talent has read the map too: the creator of the most-watched series in streaming history put $3 million of his own money not into a production company but into Twelve Labs, an AI video-understanding startup — a working showrunner going long the tooling layer.363

But television also minted the period’s genuinely novel underwriting peril. When Amazon’s AI Creators Fund commissioned three generative animated series in May and one of them — Punky Duck, from a beloved human animator — collapsed within forty-eight hours of announcement under online derision, before a frame existed, the industry learned that the audience-enforcement mechanism Chapter 5 described operating on finished work can operate on a press release.364 Insurers have categories for weather, injury, bankruptcy and war. There is no category for the commission was culturally repudiated at the moment of its announcement — and until there is, every AI-adjacent greenlight carries an unpriceable tail that has nothing to do with whether the work would have been good.

The headline television story, though, is where the exiting capital landed — because it did not leave the sector. It moved down the duration curve, hard, into the vertical microdrama: phone-native serials of sixty to a hundred one-to-two-minute episodes, budgeted at one to two hundred thousand dollars a series, shot in days, monetised coin by coin. The numbers have gone from curiosity to category in eight quarters. Category app revenue ran from roughly $178 million in the first quarter of 2024 to nearly $700 million a year later; Deloitte projects in-app microdrama revenue around $7.8 billion for 2026, more than doubling year on year; ReelShort alone booked around $400 million in 2024 revenue, still loss-making on user-acquisition spend, while DramaBox turned profitable and went seeking $100 million at a half-billion valuation; ByteDance entered the international market; TikTok quietly launched a standalone microdrama app.365 Hollywood veterans are placing what the trade openly calls big-money bets on the format precisely as the long-form shoots dry up; Fox took its equity stake in Holywater — the deal Issue 3 flagged back in October — and committed to two hundred shows in two years; one producer called verticals the first new professional format since reality television, while the legacy distributors, to their evident discomfort, sit out a market their sales model cannot parse — even as Netflix itself, in the plans Issue 26 logged, moves to add a vertical feed with AI-driven recommendation to its own app.366 When the incumbent that ended the last format war starts rebuilding its interface around the challenger’s format, the migration is no longer avant-garde.

I want to name what this actually is, because the trade coverage keeps misfiling it as a taste story. It is a duration story. Capital fleeing three-year commissions it cannot underwrite has discovered a format whose entire production-and-payback cycle fits inside the visibility window — weeks from greenlight to revenue data, unit costs two orders of magnitude below episodic television, demand legible almost in real time. Call it duration arbitrage: the reallocation of creative capital towards formats whose cycles are shorter than the uncertainty horizon. And notice the second-order behaviour already emerging, because it is the market inventing, bottom-up, exactly the instrument this chapter has been arguing the long formats lack: vertical series are beginning to function as proof-of-concept layers, where audience response and narrative traction justify longer-form investment.367 That is staged, real-options greenlighting — priced discovery before irreversible commitment — built not by the studios’ structured-finance teams but by an app economy that never read Dixit and Pindyck. The AI layer is arriving on schedule too — by late July, Nikkei was reporting from inside China’s boom on AI moviemakers chasing “2 minutes of fame,” a fully synthetic tier maturing inside the format368 — which means the microdrama market is about to run the Chapter 5 experiment — flood, ceiling, premium — at compressed speed, on the shortest cycle in scripted entertainment. Watch it the way we watched music.

The television verdict, then: the sector where AI’s investment impact is least about refusal and most about re-sorting — pipelines quietly re-tooled, announcement-stage peril priced in blood once, and the commissioning dollar migrating down the duration curve to wherever the future is visible from.

Immersive: the inversion

And then there is immersive — the sector this book comes home to — where the story runs backwards, and where reading it backwards matters most, because immersive is the clearest evidence that the duration discount is a map and not a mood.

Begin with the humiliation of the old thesis. The 2014-vintage immersive investment case was platform-led: fund the headset, the OS, the walled garden, and the content economy follows. A decade and colossal sums later, that case is being carried out of the building — Meta cutting a tenth of Reality Labs, as Chapter 14 noted, after cumulative losses that dwarf most national film funds; Apple’s headset repositioned as a beachhead rather than a mass platform, its most quietly significant feature, as Chapter 9 observed, being that its Personas run on Gaussian splatting.369 Meanwhile the experience-led immersive economy — the one that sells tickets rather than devices — has been compounding through the exact months the flat-screen sectors repriced. Sphere’s $2.3 billion Las Vegas build has become, in its investors’ own letters, a story about strong underlying unit economics; Abu Dhabi’s culture-and-tourism department is putting $1.7 billion of construction capital into a second Sphere on Yas Island for 2029; Maryland has assembled roughly $200 million in incentives for a smaller-format third; the stated ambition is a global network of venues.370 Netflix — the same balance sheet running the Dahl-and-InterPositive barbell — opened its first permanent physical destination in Philadelphia in November, with Dallas and Las Vegas to follow: a streamer converting IP into place.371 Universal’s Epic Universe set the technical bar for the park industry in the same period, and the location-based trade grew its own convention by half.372

Why does venue-scale immersive clear a discount that is strangling screen media? Three reasons, and they are this book’s themes wearing hard hats. First, the revenue is un-floodable: a ticketed, capacity-constrained physical experience is the one entertainment product to which the marginal cost of synthetic content is irrelevant — you cannot slop a building. Second, it is provenance-native: presence is its own verification, the Authenticity Premium with a postcode; the audience contract of Chapter 13 is enforced by the door. Third, look at who carries the duration — a sovereign tourism strategy, a US state’s incentive package, a franchise balance sheet — and you find the games pattern again: the long-duration bets still being made across this entire economy are held by state capital, sovereign capital, or fandom moats. Venture appears nowhere on that list. That is the chapter’s unifying empirical law, and immersive states it in concrete and steel.

Now the AI part, which is where the inversion completes. For the entire history of the discipline, the binding constraint on immersive — the reason venue content refreshes slowly, the reason virtual production stayed expensive, the reason XR content economics never closed — has been the cost of building navigable worlds. Chapter 9 described what happened to that constraint: world models collapsed it. The cost of “a place” — persistent, lit, navigable — fell one to two orders of magnitude in twelve months; Sony’s virtual-production team quoted a fortyfold speedup; Netflix’s Eyeline shipped live-action-to-4D conversion; the environment stage left the critical path.373 What belongs in this chapter is the capital’s response, because the spatial layer is where the biggest creative-technology cheques of 2026 are landing, and the newsletter caught nearly all of them as they fell. World Labs’ further $1 billion — Issue 19’s lead — at a reported valuation near $5 billion, anchored by Autodesk’s largest startup investment ever, with NVIDIA, AMD and Fidelity alongside; Odyssey’s $310 million at $1.45 billion, logged in Issue 35 the week it closed, with Amazon and GV aboard; Tripo AI’s near-$200 million for AI 3D and world-model tech in Issue 32; Yann LeCun’s AMI Labs reportedly closing a $1.03 billion seed — the largest in European history; DeepMind shipping Genie 3; NVIDIA’s Cosmos passing two million downloads.374 Beneath the spatial layer, the operating layer capitalised on the same curve: ComfyUI, the open-source node graph that Issue 1 recorded raising $17 million to build an operating system for creative AI, crossed four million users and a $500 million valuation by early summer.375 Strip the robotics framing off the world-model rounds and note what the products export to: Unreal, Unity, WebXR — the immersive toolchain. The tooling end of the barbell and the experience end of the barbell are, in immersive alone, pointing at the same future.

So the immersive verdict inverts the others. In film, television and games, AI is the reason capital cannot price the terminal market, and long-form content pays the discount. In immersive, AI is the thing that finally breaks the sector’s historic cost constraint, in service of a revenue model the flood cannot reach. The same technology that reprices flat media down on uncertainty reprices spatial media up on feasibility. The duration discount, applied across the whole map, changes sign exactly once — and it does so in the sector where the UK, through CoSTAR’s labs and networks and the R&D infrastructure this book’s programmes plug into, and through simulation champions like PhysicsX with its $300 million raise, has genuine positions on the board.376 That is either the best-timed industrial bet British creative policy has made in a generation, or an accident it should hurry to claim.

The map, read whole

Lay the four verdicts side by side and the Seven-Year Problem stops being a mood and becomes a mechanism you can read.

Games: the deepest venture repricing, capital rotated to tooling and to the industry’s own data exhaust, long duration held only by fandom moats and sovereign patience — a $55 billion LBO in which AI is simultaneously the anxiety and the margin story servicing the debt. Film: the intermediation lattice seized at the bond, the spread inverted towards anything AI-branded, an AI-native studio class capitalised from £9 million seeds to $250 million launches inside eight months, the cost curve collapsing to fourteen cents a second and $400,000 compute lines, the tooling pure-plays compounding under a hyperscaler shadow, and financing regressing to prizes and patronage where underwriting cannot form. Television: the fastest visible re-sorting — pipelines re-tooled, one commission killed by its own press release, and the money running down the duration curve into a format whose whole cycle fits inside the visibility window, inventing real-options greenlighting from below as it goes. Immersive: the inversion — un-floodable, provenance-native revenue meeting the one AI capability that dissolves the sector’s historic constraint, with states and sovereigns carrying the venue duration that venture will not touch.

One mechanism generates all four: capital pricing cannot know as will end, then seeking whatever combination of shorter duration, harder moat, or longer-horizon balance sheet lets a deal clear anyway. And one casualty recurs in every sector, which is why I keep returning to it: the middle. The unproven studio’s first game; the mid-budget original feature; the returning-series bet on a new voice; the independent immersive production between the art installation and the theme park. Chapter 13 showed the Authenticity Premium accruing to the top and the long tail and weakly to the middle; Chapter 7 showed the middle most exposed to substitution; this chapter adds the third front — the middle is also, definitionally, the longest-duration claim in the market, originality being a bet on a future taste landscape with no catalogue floor beneath it. Squeezed from below by substitution, from the side by the premium’s distribution, from above by capital’s flight from duration. Three independent mechanisms, one victim — and the victim is where every franchise on the safe end of the barbell originally came from. Even the talent has begun saying it out loud: Brad Pitt, in August, argued that AI “used as a tool” could help more mid-budget films get made377 — an actor reading the same map this chapter has been reading, and volunteering the machine as the middle’s least-bad financier. A capital regime that funds only proven IP and the tools to exploit it eats its seed corn with perfect quarterly discipline: rational for every allocator, ruinous for the system, which is the classic signature of a coordination failure and the classic licence for policy.

Which is why the instruments agenda matters more than any forecast, and why the UK’s position is more interesting — and more precarious — than its headline numbers. The Sector Plan’s finance package — the British Business Bank backing creative-sector venture managers, the expanded equity and debt funds, the exploration of IP-backed lending, the clusters money, CoSTAR’s expansion, the mayoral funds — reads, squinted at, like a portfolio of proto-duration-instruments: public capital groping towards exactly the tranche private underwriting has repriced away.378

But hold the scales up honestly, because the newsletter’s own record does. The state has just found £1.1 billion for an AI hardware plan; the Arts Council’s cumulative funding for AI-and-creativity projects since 2019 stands at £4 million; and a typical creative-AI intervention is a £3 million feasibility pot for SMEs — sums that the spatial layer’s private rounds exceed before lunch on an ordinary Tuesday.379 A country that can mobilise a billion for silicon but four million over six years for the culture the silicon is meant to serve has not yet understood which of its constraints is binding. And two structural problems remain. The instruments are underspecified — IP-backed lending is, even to sympathetic legal readers, a concept in search of a mechanism.380 And the whole edifice rests on the foundation Chapter 6 documented: a training-data property regime not merely undecided but contested, 88 per cent of consultation respondents backing full licensing against a government preference that drew 3 — which means the legal status of the very collateral the lending schemes would secure against cannot currently be priced by anyone.381 You cannot build duration instruments on a property regime the public is still fighting the government over.

The industry has solved instrument problems before — completion bonds made an uninsurable business bankable, slates made heavy-tailed demand investable, presales converted unknowable box office into contracted cash flow, and television’s vertical market is right now building priced-discovery greenlighting from spare parts. The next generation is visible in outline: staged real-options commitments for long formats; AI-era completion underwriting that can price generative pipelines, vendor mortality and announcement-stage repudiation; provenance as collateral, where the Chapter 13 verification stack meets IP-backed lending and the Authenticity Premium becomes a balance-sheet line; and public co-investment explicitly mandated to hold the middle until private books can mark it again.

The caveats, before the corollary, because the book should not over-claim and a chapter accusing the market of unfalsifiable nerves had better state its own falsifiers. This argument fails if genuine, non-fraudulent consumption of fully synthetic content breaks decisively above its current sub-one-per-cent asymptote and climbs — watch the stream-share number, never the upload number. It fails if the youth scepticism gradient of Chapter 13 reverses as the models improve, because that gradient is the premium’s demographic engine. It fails if franchise premiums compress through the flood, which would mean attention is not pooling at the lighthouses after all. And it fails, in its immersive limb, if world-model economics turn out to serve robotics and simulation while leaving venue content costs untouched — watch whether the splat pipelines actually ship inside experiences. Four dials. As of this writing, none is moving the bears’ way.

The corollary

The question from those three rooms — won’t AI have taken over by the time this ships? — turns out to have four answers, none of which is yes, and none of which is the reassurance the question was fishing for either.

In games, the honest answer is: by then, the only balance sheets left holding your kind of bet may be sovereign ones — so know whose patience you are borrowing, and know that your audience’s play may be worth more to capital than your game. In film: by then the machinery, not the audience, will have decided what got made — so the fight that matters is over underwriting criteria, not opinions, and a prize is not a financing system. In television: by then the market will have quietly rebuilt greenlighting as staged discovery — the format war is a duration war wearing a content costume. And in immersive: by then the same technology everyone else is fleeing will have made your sector’s oldest constraint optional — the taking-over, there, is the opportunity.

Capital has not concluded that AI wins. It has concluded that it cannot know, and it prices cannot know as will end — everywhere except where a moat, a sovereign, or a shortened cycle lets it stop pretending to know at all. The most expensive position in a transition is not the wrong bet. It is the unpriced one. The sectors, institutions and countries that answer the Seven-Year Problem with instruments will finance the next thirteen-year bet — and will get to decide, in the Chapter 16 sense of agency, attribution, access and audience, what kind of creative economy that bet is made inside. The ones that answer it with vibes, bullish or bearish, will discover they have outsourced that decision to whoever was left holding the term sheets.

One more thing belongs at the end of this chapter, because it is the bridge to the next one. The immersive inversion — the single place on the map where the discount changes sign — is not an accident of venue economics. It is capital noticing, earlier than most of the culture, the deepest technical shift this book tracks: that the machines have stopped making pictures and started making places. The biggest creative-technology cheques of 2026 are not chasing a better video model. They are chasing the thing underneath video — and to see why, you have to look at a release that produced no viral clips, changed no news cycle for a single day, and may matter more than everything that did.

Theoretical apparatus from the standard literature: Frank Knight, “Risk, Uncertainty and Profit” (1921); Avinash Dixit and Robert Pindyck, “Investment Under Uncertainty” (1994); Arthur De Vany, “Hollywood Economics” (2004); William Goldman, “Adventures in the Screen Trade” (1983); Mark Carney, “Breaking the Tragedy of the Horizon” (2015); William Baumol on cost disease (1966).

Chapter 9 — Worlds, Not Pictures

If you had asked me, in the autumn of 2025, what the most important AI release of the year was going to be, I would have said something obvious — Sora 2, or Veo 3.1, or one of the music models, or one of the editor-class tools like Runway Gen-4.5 or Adobe’s new Firefly. Something that turned a prompt into a thing you could put on a screen.

Six months later, I don’t think I would say any of those.

I think the most important release of the period this book covers was something that almost nobody outside of a relatively small community of practitioners noticed at the time, that produced no viral videos, that did not change the news cycle for a single day, and that I have come, over the course of the winter, to think of as the actual future of creative work: the public launch of Marble, by Fei-Fei Li’s company World Labs, in November 2025.382

Marble doesn’t make videos. Marble makes worlds.

I want to spend this chapter on why that distinction is, in my view, the most strategically important one in creative AI right now, and why almost everything else in the toolchain — from generative video to AI music to the digital-human work in advertising — eventually has to be re-thought in its shadow.

What a world model actually is

The phrase “world model” sounds like a marketing term. It isn’t, exactly. It is a category of AI system that researchers have been chasing for the better part of a decade, and that — as of late 2025 — finally started shipping as production-ready software.

A generative video model takes a prompt and produces a sequence of frames. The frames are coherent because the model has learned the statistical regularities of video: things move smoothly, light behaves more or less correctly, faces stay faces. But the output is flat. It is a particular sequence of pixels. You cannot navigate it. You cannot move the camera. You cannot pick up the lamp on the table and look at the wall behind it.

A world model takes a prompt — or an image, or a video, or a rough 3D layout — and produces a navigable three-dimensional environment. You can move through it. You can change the camera angle. You can, depending on the model, walk around the table, look at the wall behind the lamp, and find that the wall continues to exist in a consistent way that the model didn’t have to generate for you because it understood, structurally, that walls have backs.

The technical core, in the most common implementation, is Gaussian splatting — a representation where a scene is stored as a cloud of millions of tiny semi-transparent ellipsoids, each carrying colour and position information. The whole scene can be rendered in real time from any angle, because the system isn’t drawing 2D pixels; it is rendering a structured 3D world. The output, in turn, can be exported as a splat file, as a mesh, or — if you want — as a flat video.383

This is the part that took me, even as a working creative technologist, embarrassingly long to fully understand. Video is a projection of a world. A world is the more fundamental object. For two and a half years, the public-facing AI conversation has been about generating better projections. The actual capability landscape has been moving, in parallel, towards generating the worlds themselves.

When the worlds become cheap to generate, the projections — the videos, the images, the renders — become outputs of the worlds, not the primary medium. The whole production stack inverts.

Marble, from the inside

DreamLab — the studio I run in the North West of the UK — has been a beta participant in Marble since October 2025, in the months before its public release.384 I want to share what that experience actually felt like, because the technical description of a world model and the practitioner’s experience of using one are different in ways that matter for understanding what is happening to the toolchain.

Imagine, for the sake of example, that I am working on a client project that needs a scene of a market square at dusk in a Mediterranean town. In the old pipeline — which is to say, the pipeline of 2024 and most of 2025 — that brief would translate into something like the following:

A concept artist would produce a moodboard. A 3D artist or a virtual-production house would build a CGI version of the square, populated with assets either bought from a marketplace or modelled bespoke. Lighting would be set up in Unreal or Maya. The whole scene would be rendered out as a video plate or used as a backdrop on an LED volume. If any change was required — can we move the camera left a bit, see what’s on that side — the rebuild was non-trivial.

In Marble, the same brief unfolds differently. I type, or paste in a reference image, or upload a quick phone-shot panorama of an actual market square I visited last year. Marble generates a complete, navigable 3D environment of that square. It exists, persistently, as a file on my account. I can move my virtual camera anywhere in it. I can hand it to a director and say walk through this and tell me where the camera lives. I can export the result as a Gaussian splat, drop it into Unreal Engine via SuperSplat or one of the other Gaussian-splat editors,385 and use it as the lit backdrop for an LED-volume shoot. I can also, if I just want a plate, render a flat video from a chosen camera move.

The economic implication is this: the cost of having “a place” — a navigable, lit, persistent environment with depth — has dropped, in twelve months, by something between one and two orders of magnitude. The thing that used to require a four-person team and a fortnight now requires a prompt and the time it takes a model to render.

This is not a marginal improvement to virtual production. It is a category change. The bottleneck of virtual production has, for the entire history of the discipline, been the cost and time of building the environment. When that bottleneck goes, what remains is exactly the human craft that the audience is paying for: blocking, performance, direction, lighting design, story.

In Issue 8 of the newsletter, I noted that Sony Pictures had begun using Marble inside its virtual-production pipeline. The number the team quoted publicly was the one that should have made the front page of every trade publication: 40× faster than the traditional workflow.386 If you sit inside the legacy economics of a virtual-production house — where building a single environment is a six-figure, multi-week proposition — that number is not an improvement. It is a re-platforming of the discipline. In Issue 12, Disney showed off a “300,000 poses in an instant” demonstration that was conceptually similar — animation built on top of generative spatial infrastructure rather than against it.387 In Issue 27, Netflix and Eyeline released Vista4D, a system that converts live-action footage into navigable 4D point clouds.388 The pattern is the same across the studios: a quiet pipeline shift, not a marketing story, that takes the entire “building the environment” stage out of the critical path of production.

The world-model race

Marble was the first commercial product in this category, but it was not the only one. The autumn of 2025 and the spring of 2026 were essentially a foot-race between research labs to ship usable world models, and the pace of releases was so rapid that the Dream Machine readers’ WhatsApp group routinely had three or four new ones to discuss per week.

Google DeepMind’s Genie 3, named by Time as one of the best inventions of 2025, generated playable 3D worlds at 24 frames per second from text prompts, with consistency held for several minutes — and in January 2026 was made publicly available to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. through a prototype web app called Project Genie. At Google I/O 2026, Project Genie was extended with a Street View integration that lets users generate navigable simulations of real-world locations directly from Street View map data, collapsing the gap between the world that exists and the world that can be generated.389 Meta announced WorldGen in November 2025, framed as research that could generate walkable 3D worlds from prompts like “medieval village town square.”390 Tencent open-sourced HY World 1.5, a real-time world model framework, in December 2025, alongside the Hunyuan 3D Studio which integrated the company’s art-grade 3D generative model 3D-PolyGen 1.5.391 SpAItial launched ECHO, a spatial foundation model, in December 2025.392 Stanford AI Lab and others released Wonderzoom in January 2026, a multi-scale 3D world-generation model that let you “infinitely zoom into the details” of a generated environment.393 OpenArt launched its own world-generation product, Worlds, in March 2026.394

The May 2026 wave was the most aggressive yet. NVIDIA released SANA-WM, a 2.6B-parameter open-source world model natively trained for 60-second video generation with explicit camera control — the first open-weight world model at meaningful scale, and a development whose long-term implications for the open-source-AI-tooling argument I make in Chapter 17 are, in my view, substantial.395 Odyssey released Starchild-1, which it described as “the first ever real-time multimodal world model” — a system that doesn’t just generate a world but understands and simulates it.396 A month later, Odyssey closed a $310 million Series B explicitly framed as capital to accelerate its world models — which is, for anyone still wondering whether the spatial thesis is a niche enthusiasm, the sound of the capital markets pricing it in.397 Apple published Headsup, a large-scale, high-quality 3D Gaussian-head reconstruction pipeline built from multi-view captures of the kind a consumer iPhone can already produce — a continuation of the Apple-Personas-and-Gaussian-splat thread above.398 At the consumer end of the same wave, WorldLens VR rolled out an AI-powered Quest feature that adds subtle 3D depth to ordinary Google Street View environments, making the existing planetary-scale street-imagery dataset navigable in VR.399

The most ambitious of all of these — and the one I think hints most clearly at where the category is going — was Luma AI’s UNI-1, launched in March 2026 with the framing: “When worlds become instant, the race shifts to better thinking.”400 UNI-1 was the first commercial release I am aware of that combined world-model generation with what Luma called “reasoning” — that is, the model didn’t just generate a scene, it could plan, modify and iterate on the scene as a coherent agent. The pitch was that you would no longer have a fragmented pipeline of prompt → image → video → iterate; you would have a single unified creative system that thought before it created.

UNI-1 is, in my view, the most important category announcement of the spring of 2026, even if the product itself is still rough at the edges. It is the announcement that says: world models are not the end state. They are the substrate on which something else — reasoning-led generative creativity — gets built.

By May 2026, you could find world-model capabilities embedded in the consumer tools as well. CapCut, the consumer-grade video editing app, integrated ByteDance’s Seedance 2.0 via the Dreamina product, giving phone-users the ability to generate spatial scenes alongside flat video.401 Spark 2.0, an open-source Gaussian-splat streaming framework, brought 100-million-splat scenes to web browsers at interactive frame rates.402 Apple confirmed in October 2025 that its Personas feature on Vision Pro and other devices was powered by Gaussian splatting under the hood, making this — for the millions of Apple device owners who had used the feature without knowing what it was — the most-deployed Gaussian-splat technology in consumer hardware.403

The category, in eight months, went from a research demo to a consumer feature.

And then, over the summer of 2026, it went from a race to a crowd. Adobe — the company whose entire franchise has been the flat canvas — showed Wonder, a real-time interactive 3D world-navigation model out of Adobe Research, in July.404 Tencent followed its HY World line with WorldClaw, an agentic system for generating 3D open worlds at scale — worlds built by agents in bulk rather than prompted into existence one at a time.405 The smaller labs kept pace: Reactor’s LingBot-World 2.0 did real-time world generation,406 and AlayaWorld pushed long-horizon playable video worlds.407 Wayve — an autonomous-driving company — shipped GAIA-4, the latest of its world models, which is worth pausing on: the same category of system that generates a market square for a film shoot is being built, in parallel, to teach cars what streets are.408 The physical-AI end of that same thread showed up in August, when Niantic Spatial — the spatial-mapping company carved out of the Pokémon Go empire — began building the city of Rancho Cordova’s digital twin as foundation infrastructure for physical AI: capture a real place once, and everything downstream, from robots to route-planning to broadcast, renders from the model rather than from the world.409 And in August, Lightricks released LTX-2.5 as an open-source open-world model — the SANA-WM moment repeating itself, as open weights always eventually arrive downstream of the frontier.410 I am keeping this deliberately compressed — the full inventory lives in Chapter 17 — because the point is not any single model. The point is that in thirteen months the world model went from one company’s strange conviction to the assumed next platform of an entire industry, with Adobe, Tencent, an autonomous-driving lab and the open-source community all arriving at the same destination from four different directions.

The splat pipeline underneath it matured in the same weeks. In July 2026 alone, Gracia AI brought 4D Gaussian splats — splats with a time dimension; volumetric video you can walk around — into Unreal Engine with real-time relighting and self-shadowing; Atlux shipped the reverse trip, Unreal-to-4DGS; and Notch, a staple tool of the live-events and concert-visuals world, added native splat import and rendering.411 The capture side compressed just as dramatically. InfiniSplat, a SIGGRAPH Asia system, turns a single photograph into a navigable 3DGS scene;412 and the Insta360 X6 — a consumer 360 camera — shipped a feature called Spatial Capture: record a place in 360, open the app, and the place becomes a 3D model.413 Read those two together and the direction is unmistakable. The world model’s input is becoming anything — one image, one walk-through with a camera you can buy on the high street — and its output is becoming a first-class citizen of every professional pipeline that used to speak only polygons.

The games industry, again

If world models are infrastructure, the industry that has been waiting for that infrastructure the longest is games.

The 2024 conversation in games about generative AI was, in significant part, about flat assets — concept art, textures, dialogue, music — and it was the conversation that produced most of the backlash. Call of Duty: Black Ops 7’s loading screens. Anno 117’s placeholder art “slipping through” the review process. Fortnite’s Chapter 8 controversy.414 The audience response, in every case, was visceral, and the studios learned, the hard way, that AI-generated 2D assets dropped into established franchises read to fans as a cost-cutting move, not a creative one.

The 2025–26 conversation in games is different in kind, because the AI is now being aimed at the substrate of the game — the worlds, the systems, the NPCs, the procedural infrastructure — and the audience response is, so far, much more nuanced.

NVIDIA, in partnership with Stanford, released NitroGen in January 2026 — a “plays-any-game” AI trained on 40,000 hours of gameplay across more than 1,000 games. The model wasn’t being pitched as a way to replace games; it was being pitched as the foundation layer for a new generation of AI-aware game agents and procedural systems.415 Google DeepMind’s SIMA 2, released in November 2025, was an agent that could play, reason and learn alongside humans in virtual 3D environments.416 Ubisoft open-sourced its CHORD model in December 2025, for end-to-end PBR material generation, and ComfyUI nodes built on top of it within the same week.417 Ubisoft’s Teammates — a voice AI tech demo first shown in November 2025 — promised a step-change in how NPCs would behave in next-generation titles. The team lead’s hands-on framing, given to Video Games Chronicle, is the one I keep returning to: “It’s a tool first. We’ve been working on it for more than two years now, and our conclusion is that it’s a super cool tool, but it’s still a tool.”418 Still a tool. The whole AI-in-games debate, compressed into four words by the people inside Ubisoft who are actually building the thing.

The most interesting single release of the spring of 2026 was YouTube’s Playables Builder, a closed-beta product launched in December 2025 that lets users create games with short text, video or image prompts, built on Gemini 3.419 The framing, when YouTube’s product team described it publicly, was that every YouTube creator should have the ability to ship a playable game as easily as they currently ship a video. Within months, Unity announced an “AI Open Beta” — an in-editor AI suite that brought the same logic to the professional games-development pipeline.420

By June 2026 the prompt-to-playable category had stopped being a YouTube curiosity and become a product race. The Sandbox announced The Sandbox Studio, pitched as taking a creator from idea to live multiplayer game in hours;421 a week later Higgsfield — the AI-video company whose commercial numbers I return to in Chapter 10 — introduced Higgsfield Games, a system that promises to create and deploy multiplayer games from a single prompt.422 And at the State of Unreal, Epic showed where the professional engine layer is heading: Unreal MCP, LLM-powered tools and video-model integrations that let creators direct the engine through natural language. The debate that followed — would this hollow out the craft of Blueprints? — rather missed what I take to be Epic’s actual bet: not replacing developers but expanding who can become one, growing the whole creator ecosystem across games, film and immersive by lowering the technical barrier to entry.423

The platform that has been most explicit about the destination is Roblox. In June 2026 it acquired three AI research teams — Morpheus AI, Dynamics Lab and Lucid AI — in a single consolidating move aimed, in the company’s own framing, at solving the specific technical problems blocking photorealistic multiplayer worlds.424 Morpheus builds video world models using Self Forcing, a technique for converting offline video models into fast, autoregressive, interactive engines. Read the acquisition list as a sentence and it says: the largest user-generated-worlds platform on Earth believes the world model is its next rendering engine, and it is buying the research capacity to build it.

Where this lands, in 2027 and 2028, is the question I find the most strategically charged in the whole industry. If creating a playable, navigable world becomes a thing a YouTube creator can do in an afternoon, the boundary between games and video — which has been collapsing slowly for fifteen years, through platforms like Roblox and Fortnite and the proliferation of interactive content on social platforms — collapses fully. The next generation of creators will not think in terms of making a video or making a game. They will think in terms of making a thing, and the thing will, by default, be navigable.

The storyworld, live: the 2026 World Cup

In June 2026, while the tool announcements were stacking up, the thesis of this chapter received its first field test at genuinely planetary scale — and it came not from a studio, a lab or a games platform, but from football.

The 2026 FIFA World Cup — 48 teams, 104 matches, sixteen cities across three countries, an audience of six billion — is, on the evidence I assembled for the newsletter’s Deep Dive that month, the largest live deployment of AI in entertainment history.425 Before kicking a ball, every one of the tournament’s 1,248 players stood still for one second while a scanner built a photorealistic digital twin — a 3D avatar that then spent the following five weeks adjudicating offsides, driving broadcast replays and populating immersive experiences. Combine the scanned avatars with a sensor-carrying match ball and computer-vision tracking across the stadium camera arrays, and something structurally new happens to the broadcast: the match is no longer merely captured by cameras. It exists as a live data model that can be analysed, visualised and re-rendered from almost any perspective — including perspectives no physical camera ever occupied.

Stop and notice what that is. It is the inversion this chapter has been describing, running live in front of most of the connected human species. The world — the match, the stadium, the twenty-two tracked bodies — is the fundamental object. The television picture is one projection of it. The automated offside decision is another. The 3D replay on the BBC is a third. And the tournament’s second venue is a fourth: the official FIFA World Cup experience on Roblox, the platform’s biggest sports activation to date, which by the tournament’s opening weeks had logged over 1.1 billion visits — with real-time standings piping the actual tournament into the game world so the virtual carnival tracks the real one match by match.426 For a generation of Gen Z and Alpha fans, that voxel stadium, not the broadcast, is where the World Cup is happening.

Around the canonical event, the halo: TikTok as FIFA’s “preferred platform” with thirty Creator Correspondents, archival footage licensed to creators for co-creation, AI-personalised highlight packages assembled end-to-end for each fan’s declared teams and interests, machine translation and auto-clipping collapsing the gap between the final whistle and the posted edit. The World Cup is not an event with media coverage any more. It is a storyworld — one scarce, live, unscripted core wrapped in an infinitely expanding, AI-mediated halo of derivative worlds, each surface rendering the same underlying reality for a different audience, in a different grammar, at a different depth. That architecture is, I would bet, the template every major cultural property chases for the next decade — and the next generation of entertainment franchises will not bolt a transmedia strategy on after the fact; they will be designed as storyworlds from inception, built to be captured once and rendered everywhere. The officiating stack, the stadium digital twins, the creator economy and the synthetic-rights precedents being set in the players’ contracts each reward closer study, and the fuller treatment sits in DreamLab’s published research on the tournament.

The physical venue layer, meanwhile, is moving the same way at its own pace: the same month, Sphere announced that The Rocky Horror Picture Show would be re-worked with “advanced technologies” into an immersive experience for the Las Vegas venue — a fifty-year-old flat film being promoted, in effect, into a place you stand inside.427

What this means for film

I want to come back to film for a moment, because I think the consequences of world models for the film industry are bigger than the consequences for any other sector, and the least understood.

For the entire history of cinema, the discipline has been organised around a fundamental scarcity: the cost of building the location. Even when the location was real — a city street, a forest, a beach — capturing it required a crew, a lighting team, transport, permits, weather contingencies. When it wasn’t real — when it was a sound stage, or a digital matte painting, or a CGI environment — the cost was, if anything, higher.

The entire industrial structure of cinema, from the location department to the gaffer’s crew to the virtual-production house, exists because the place is expensive to make.

When the place becomes cheap — when a Marble-generated environment, exported as a splat, dropped into Unreal, lit interactively, can substitute for a $200,000-per-day exterior shoot at almost any quality bar a hero shot — the industrial structure that organised cinema starts to look like the manuscript-copying scriptorium did in 1450. The thing that was the bottleneck is no longer the bottleneck.

What replaces it? My best guess, six months into the transition, is taste in places. If everyone can generate a market square, the value of choosing the right market square — the one with the texture, the light, the cultural specificity, the lived-in-ness that makes a scene feel like it belongs to a real human story — becomes the new scarce skill. The location scout becomes the world curator. The production designer becomes the spatial director. The cinematographer becomes — even more than they already are — the person whose job is to find the one camera move in a near-infinite navigable space that tells the story.

This is, I think, an upgrade for the craft, not a downgrade. It moves the human contribution to the part of the work that humans actually do well — judgement about what matters in a place — and offloads the part of the work that has been a manufacturing problem for a hundred years.

The risk

I want to flag the risk too, because I am trying — and I am sure I will not always succeed — to be honest about the downsides.

If world models become the substrate of creative work, the training data for those models becomes a question of enormous cultural consequence. A world model trained on, say, the visual archive of Hollywood will generate scenes that look like Hollywood. A world model trained on the photographic archive of Mumbai will generate scenes that look like Mumbai. The aesthetic monoculture that the early image-generation models produced — that vaguely Pixar-flavoured, vaguely Marvel-flavoured, vaguely YouTube-thumbnail look that you can recognise in a thousand 2024 AI outputs at a glance — is at risk of being amplified, not reduced, when the medium moves from images to navigable spaces.

The companies that own the largest world-model training datasets in 2030 will, in a real sense, own the visual language of the next generation of cinema, games and immersive media. If those datasets are biased — towards English, towards the global North, towards Hollywood production design, towards the architectural and cultural visual vocabulary of a small number of wealthy cities — the entire interior life of the next generation of creative work will reflect those biases.

This is not a hypothetical. We are seeing it now. The publicly available world models, in mid-2026, do a startlingly good job of generating “Mediterranean market square” and “American suburb” and “Tokyo street at night.” They do a startlingly thin job of generating, say, “Lagos street at dusk during the rains” or “a contemporary Indigenous Australian community space” or “a Manchester terraced street in winter with the sodium lights coming on.” The bias is in the training, and the training is in the assets, and the assets were in the corpus, and the corpus was English-internet-skewed.

If we want the next creative economy to look like the world rather than like the AI companies’ biggest source datasets, the dataset question has to be a first-order design problem. Korin AI’s late-2025 launch — “trained with African datasets, built by Africans” — is the kind of intervention that is going to have to multiply.428 So is the African Tech / India / Singapore-led wave of culturally-specific AI cinema that the trade press started covering in Issues 20 through 27. Diversity in training datasets, for the world-model era, is not a content-moderation question. It is a cultural infrastructure question.

Six craft questions for the world-model era

Before I make the big claim, I want to put six craft questions on the page that working creatives — directors, designers, art directors, cinematographers, sound designers, level designers — will, by my estimate, be wrestling with for the rest of the decade. They are the world-model-era equivalents of the craft questions the cinematographic era took fifty years to develop a vocabulary for (where do you put the camera, how do you light the scene, how does the cut work, how does the sound do its work). The world-model era has, in 2026, no settled vocabulary for any of them. The vocabulary will be built by the working creatives who notice the question first.

One. Where does the audience stand? The most-overlooked craft question of the navigable-space era. A film positions the camera; the camera positions the audience. A world model produces a navigable space; the question of where the audience enters the space, where they are invited to stand, what they are encouraged to look at, is no longer fixed by the cinematographer. It is fixed — if it is fixed at all — by the narrative scaffolding the orchestrator builds around the navigable space. Marble’s October-2025 update added explicit suggested-camera-pose primitives for exactly this reason. The craft question is which of those poses to specify and which to leave to the audience.

Two. How does the cut work in a navigable scene? The film cut depends on the audience being in a fixed position; the editor moves the camera between fixed positions in a way that the audience’s eye follows. The navigable scene has, by default, no cut. The audience moves through it continuously. The craft question — for working directors and editors — is when to break the continuity, how to do so in a way the audience reads as deliberate rather than as a technical glitch, and what new grammar of transitions a navigable medium permits. Some early experiments in 2025–26 have used spatial discontinuities (an audience walks through a door and emerges in a different space) and temporal discontinuities (the same space at different times) as cuts. None of these has yet stabilised into a shared grammar.

Three. How does performance survive the medium? A film performance is captured by a camera at a fixed angle and pace. A world-model performance — a synthetic actor performing inside a navigable scene — has to be authored such that the performance works from every angle and every speed at which the audience might encounter it. This is, for working performers and motion-capture supervisors, an entirely new craft challenge. The film-era cliché of the actor “playing to the camera” is, in the world-model era, replaced by playing to the spatial neighbourhood — knowing that the audience may be six feet away, may be inside the actor’s eyeline, may be behind the actor’s shoulder, may be looking at the actor from above. Volumetric capture (Vista4D’s live-action 4D reconstruction, NVIDIA’s D-Rex digital-human pipeline) is the technical answer. The performance answer — what acting means in a medium where there is no fourth wall — has not been worked out.

Four. What does sound design do in a navigable scene? A film sound mix is, for the most part, a fixed track timed to the picture cut. A navigable-scene sound mix has to follow the audience. Spatial-audio tooling (the SonicLab SPATAI pipeline, Dolby Atmos for VR, the various Meta-and-Apple immersive-audio platforms) is the technical answer. The craft question is, again, what good spatial sound design looks like in a medium where the audience-author relationship has changed.

Five. What is the running-time of a navigable scene? A film has a fixed running time. A navigable scene does not. The audience could leave after thirty seconds or stay for two hours. The craft question for the working director is how to design the experience so that both extremes produce a satisfying piece of work. Games have, for fifty years, been grappling with this question — the Dark Souls answer (every player gets a different running time depending on skill and exploration) is different from the Outer Wilds answer (the running time is gated by narrative discovery) is different from the Telltale Games answer (the running time is broadly fixed across players). World-model cinema, in 2026, has not yet settled on its equivalent.

Six. What is the single best moment of a navigable scene? Film has scenes — discrete units of dramatic action with a recognisable shape, a recognisable peak, a recognisable end. A navigable scene, by default, does not. The craft question for the working director is whether to design the navigable scene around a single peak moment (which the audience may or may not reach) or to design it as a texture (which the audience experiences at whatever density their navigation produces). The peak-moment design pulls the medium back toward film conventions; the texture design pushes it toward something more like architecture or landscape design. Different working directors will, on the historical pattern, settle on different answers. The grammar will, over a decade, stabilise into a working vocabulary the way the cinematic-cut grammar stabilised between 1903 and 1925.

The six questions are not, in 2026, theoretical problems. They are the questions the working spatial-cinema teams I have talked to — the Wonderzoom group at Stanford, the World Labs developer cohort, the early adopters at Sony Pictures and Eyeline — are wrestling with on Wednesday afternoons. They are also, on the historical pattern of Chapter 2, the questions whose answers will define what working creatives in the next decade are paid to do. The directors and designers who develop a working vocabulary for them first will, on the available evidence, become the named Walter Murchs of the spatial-cinema era. The ones who wait for the vocabulary to settle will, in retrospect, look like the editors who waited too long to learn Avid.

The big claim

Let me make the big claim, and then move on.

I think — and this is the most non-obvious bet in this book — that the world model is the medium of the next twenty years of creative work, in the same way that the moving image was the medium of the twentieth century and the interactive screen was the medium of the first quarter of the twenty-first.

I think people who are working in flat-video, flat-image, flat-audio formats in 2030 will increasingly be working in a legacy format — still alive, still culturally valuable, still where the highest-end of the craft lives, the way live theatre or vinyl-record production still lives — while the dominant mode of creative work will be the production, curation, performance and distribution of navigable spaces.

I think the studios, platforms and tool companies that are quietly investing in world models now — World Labs, DeepMind, Meta, NVIDIA, Tencent, Luma, Apple — will be the ones that set the rails for the next two decades.

I think the audience, having developed the antibodies described in Chapter 5 to slop-grade flat AI content, will eventually develop a parallel set of tastes for navigable content — and that the question of what makes a good AI world (rather than a good AI video) will be the central craft question of the late 2020s.

And I think — most importantly for the next chapter — that the toolchain to make all of this is being built, right now, by a small number of platform companies who have started saying out loud that AI is going to be in everything, everywhere, all at once — and who are, while you are reading this paragraph, designing the rails on which the next creative economy will run.

Chapter 10 — AI in Everything, Everywhere, All at Once

In late October 2025, at Adobe MAX, the company that has made the software almost everyone in the creative industries uses every day — Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, After Effects, InDesign — decided that the year-old marketing line “AI is a feature in our tools” had outlived its usefulness, and replaced it with a more honest one.

The new line was: “AI in everything, everywhere, all at once.”429

The reason I want to spend a chapter on that phrase is not because I love a slogan. The reason I want to spend a chapter on it is that I think it is, more than any other single piece of corporate positioning from the period this book covers, literally true. AI is in everything now. It is in every layer of the creative software stack. And the implications of that for working creatives — for the way we are trained, the way we are paid, the way we work with each other — are not yet, in the spring of 2026, fully understood.

This chapter is about the platform layer. About the companies that make the tools that the rest of the creative industries use to make the work. About how those companies have, in the past eight months, accepted that their business is no longer making tools but making agents, and about what that means for the rest of us.

The Adobe MAX week

The Adobe MAX 2025 keynote — held in mid-October in Los Angeles, the week after OpenAI’s DevDay, two weeks after Tilly Norwood — was unusual, by Adobe’s standards, in how much it tried to land at once.

The headline products were Firefly Foundry, a service for companies to train their own custom generative models on their own visual identity;430 Firefly Image Model 5, the latest generation of the image generator that has, since 2023, been Adobe’s primary public answer to Midjourney and Stable Diffusion;431 and an AI Assistant built directly into Adobe Express, the company’s lower-barrier consumer creative tool.432

Underneath the headlines was a much longer list of “Project” announcements — Adobe’s research-preview format, the things that may or may not ship but that signal what the company is investing in. The list, looked at as a whole, is what convinced me, sitting at my desk in the North West watching the live stream, that something larger than a product launch was happening:

Project Scene It: image-to-3D and 3D-to-image technologies, with reference-image tagging for object preservation in 3D space.

Project Surface Swap: AI-powered material recognition, letting designers swap textures while preserving lighting, shading and perspective.

Project Turn Style: editing 2D objects as if they were 3D.

Project Trace Erase: removing objects and their shadows, reflections and environmental distortions in one operation.

Project New Depths: editing depth in an image as easily as adjusting brightness.

Project Frame Forward: applying changes across entire videos based on one annotated frame and a text prompt — “the precision of photo editing in video workflows.”

Project Motion Map: bringing static vector graphics to life automatically.

Project Sound Stager: analysing a video’s visuals, pacing and emotional tone, and automatically generating layered soundscapes.

Project Clean Take: AI correction of mispronunciations, voice isolation, noise removal and delivery refinement.

Project Graph: a node-based workflow editor, conceptually similar to ComfyUI, for chaining Adobe’s tools and models into custom pipelines.433

There is, in that list of ten projects, every layer of the post-production stack — image, video, 3D, audio, layout, workflow — being re-imagined as a generative or agentic operation. Not a tool with an AI feature stapled on. A generative-first reimagining of the operation itself.
